extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students, and practitioners interested in classical mechanics and rolling contact
extracted.subtask_description: An encyclopedia-style exposition of the physical concept of rolling: definitions, kinematics, energy, forces, special cases, applications, and contact mechanics. Aimed at teaching or referencing core principles of rolling motion in mechanics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of rolling
rubrics_metrics.description: Rolling is a type of motion that combines rotation (commonly, of an axially symmetric object) and translation of that object with respect to a surface (either one or the other moves), such that, if ideal conditions exist, the two are in contact with each other without sliding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This establishes the basic conceptual criterion for when motion is classified as rolling (a superposition of rotation and translation with contact). It notes that rolling objects need not be axially symmetric and gives examples (e.g., Reuleaux triangle, Meissner bodies).

rubrics_metrics.name: Pure rolling (no sliding)
rubrics_metrics.description: Rolling where there is no sliding is referred to as pure rolling. By definition, there is no sliding when there is a frame of reference in which all points of contact on the rolling object have the same velocity as their counterparts on the surface on which the object rolls; in particular, for a frame in which the rolling plane is at rest, the instantaneous velocity of all the points of contact of the rolling object is zero.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the frame-of-reference test (contact-point velocities equal) to determine pure rolling; instantaneous contact velocity zero in plane-rest frame is a useful practical check. The article notes that in practice micro-deformations can produce small sliding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rolling resistance vs sliding friction (practical considerations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Due to small deformations near the contact area, some sliding and energy dissipation occurs. Nevertheless, the resulting rolling resistance is much lower than sliding friction, and thus rolling objects typically require much less energy to be moved than sliding ones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains practical implications: minimize slip to reduce energy loss and loss of control (e.g., road conditions like snow, sand, oil increase slip risk). Emphasizes bearings and lubrication to reduce friction in mechanisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kinematics: point velocities and trajectories
rubrics_metrics.description: The velocities of the points of a rolling object are equal to those of rotation around the point of contact. The velocity of any point is given by v = ω × r, where r is displacement from the contact point; trajectories of points are trochoids, and points on the rim trace cycloids.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret rolling instantaneous motion as equivalent to rotation about the contact point. Use v = ω × r for velocity of any particle; expect different instantaneous directions (some points may move opposite to overall motion when below surface level).

rubrics_metrics.name: Kinetic energy decomposition for rolling bodies
rubrics_metrics.description: K_rolling = K_translation + K_rotation. Using parallel-axis theorem: K_rolling = 1/2 m v_c.o.m.^2 + 1/2 I_rotation ω^2, where v_c.o.m. = r ω for a symmetric rolling body on a flat surface.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shows how translational and rotational contributions sum; derive via parallel-axis theorem and relation between center-of-mass speed and angular velocity. Useful for comparing energetic costs of different mass distributions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dynamics: relation between linear and angular acceleration and role of friction
rubrics_metrics.description: Differentiating v_c.o.m. = r ω gives a = r α. Newton's second law and rotational dynamics imply that to accelerate a rolling object both net force and torque are required; static friction at the contact point typically provides the torque. When static friction isn't enough, slipping occurs and dynamic friction applies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides derivation linking F_net, torque τ, inertia I, and acceleration. Shows that tangential (friction) force is opposite external force direction and reduces net force; includes algebraic steps for F_net and how rotational inertia reduces linear acceleration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effective inertial term and F_net formula (I / (m r^2) factor)
rubrics_metrics.description: The net force and acceleration for a rolling object under an external force that exerts no torque are reduced by a factor that depends on the object's rotational inertia: F_net = F_external / (1 + I/(m r^2)). Equivalently, a = F_external / (m + I/r^2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interprets I/r^2 as a 'virtual mass' due to rotational inertia; introduces radius of gyration r_g = sqrt(I/m) so the denominator becomes 1 + (r_g/r)^2. Use this to reason about how mass distribution affects acceleration for the same external force.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceleration on an inclined plane (no drag, static friction only)
rubrics_metrics.description: For an object rolling down an incline with only static friction, normal force and weight (no air drag), the acceleration is a = g sin(θ) / (1 + (r_g / r)^2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derived by taking F_external = g m sin(θ) and applying the effective inertial term. Emphasizes that r_g/r depends on shape and mass distribution, and that acceleration is independent of scale/density for given shape.

rubrics_metrics.name: Special and non-axially-symmetric rollers; developable rollers
rubrics_metrics.description: Rolling objects are not necessarily axially symmetric. Examples: Reuleaux triangle, Meissner bodies. Members of 'developable rollers' (oloid, sphericon) develop their entire surface when rolling. Objects with corners (dice) roll by successive rotations about the contacting edge/corner. Specific surfaces can allow a perfect square wheel to roll with centroid at constant height.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Highlights geometric diversity of rolling bodies and non-intuitive behaviors (circular motion of cone's center of gravity, square wheel on specially constructed road). Useful when considering kinematics for nonstandard shapes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deformable bodies and contact mechanics (steady rolling)
rubrics_metrics.description: When an axisymmetric deformable body contacts a surface, an interface is formed transmitting normal and shear forces. Deformations and motions in steady rolling can be characterized using an Eulerian description of rigid body rotation combined with a Lagrangian description of deformation. Finite element analysis (steady-state rolling FEA) methods (Padovan et al.) are used for practical analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes that this approach eliminates time dependence and yields spatial fields of displacement, velocity, stress, and strain. Relevant for tires, rolling-element contact, and engineering simulations; references commercial codes and literature for implementation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical applications of rolling
rubrics_metrics.description: Most land vehicles use wheels and thus rolling for displacement. Rolling-element bearings (e.g., ball bearings) are used in rotating devices to allow low-friction rotation. Rolling is also used in transportation of objects on lined-up rollers and in processes such as metalworking, printing, rubber manufacturing, and painting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasizes design and safety considerations: minimize slip (e.g., avoid snow, sand, oil), importance of bearing quality and lubrication to control friction, and the historical/modern practical uses of rolling in machinery and transport.
